messages:
mike: quick follow-up from today's ianto RFC review — i sketched an eviction hysteresis approach for the continuous batcher, want quick feedback :thinking:

Tanya: high level please — main goal is to avoid flapping when a burst clears, right?

mike: exactly. current behavior evicts small batches aggressively to keep latency low. that causes oscillation when load is near threshold — throughput suffers because we keep rebuilding batches. hysteresis would add two thresholds: entry_threshold and exit_threshold (exit > entry) so eviction isn't immediate.

li: that makes sense. exit > entry buys stability. do we have perf model tradeoffs?

mike: short notes:
- pro: reduces churn in kernel launches, better throughput for bursty tails
- con: slightly worse 95/99 latency for very short urgent requests because they might wait longer before a batch is evicted
- pro: simpler than full token-deadline preemption initially

ryan: how does this interact with priority lanes? e.g., reserved low-latency lanes for paid customers.

mike: plan: hysteresis is per-lane. each lane has independent thresholds. higher-priority lanes have lower entry_threshold and lower exit_threshold so they evacuate faster. lower-priority have wider gap to favor throughput.

alex: curious about head-of-line blocking — if a single long seq request sits in front of many short ones, hysteresis could worsen latency. mitigation?

mike: good call. two mitigations: 1) token-budget preemption heuristic — if waiting tokens exceed budget we preempt long request (best-effort) and materialize a short tail batch. 2) size-aware admission: if a request's estimated remaining tokens > max_slot, route to long-request pool to avoid mixing. both incremental.

Tanya: can you paste the rough config snippet? would help ops review.

mike: sure:
```
continuous_batcher:
  lanes:
    - name: low_latency
      entry_threshold: 1
      exit_threshold: 2
      max_batch: 8
    - name: best_effort
      entry_threshold: 4
      exit_threshold: 12
      max_batch: 64
  preemption:
    enabled: true
    token_budget: 128
    min_preempt_delay_ms: 20
```

li: two quick thoughts: 1) make exit_threshold proportional to observed kernel startup cost (ms) + avg token hit time. 2) expose a sliding factor so we can tune across model families without redeploy.

mike: agreed. runtime can emit a "batch_efficiency" metric and we can auto-suggest exit_threshold via Optimize later.

ryan: rollout plan? small canary in us-west with p50/p95 p99 dashboards, then A/B on a single customer?

mike: yes. rollout steps: 1) feature flag + unit tests for correctness, 2) canary in us-west on production fleet for 24h, 3) A/B traffic split on non-critical tenant to measure unit-economics, 4) flip per-lane for higher tiers after success.

alex: what about experiments for extreme burst scenarios — do we simulate by replaying traces or synthetic Poisson bursts?

mike: both. we'll replay real traces (replay harness) and synthetic step bursts to test oscillation. scheduler-bot: can schedule a replay job once you upload traces. :rocket:

scheduler-bot: replay job queued: replay/1790001111-hysteresis-burst-sim (ETA ~35m)

Tanya: sounds good. next: mike, please open small RFC PR with config defaults and expected metrics (batch_efficiency, kernel_churn, preemption_count). then we'll review for release window. :thumbsup:
